title: Three meanings of error (worked out on cardboard)
note: The authored thinking for one hall, in the first person, by the pass (Claude), for Palle's request of 2026-11-14 (see Russell_Paradox.json). 'at' is the floor's own frame in metres (x east, z south), 'yaw' in degrees. A sticker of kind 'quote' stands word for word in the hall text; every other kind is mine and may be wrong - the plates say where I am unsure.

hero.why: The hall text is about this one exhibit: three sheets that score a straight-line fit to the same observations under three rules, a point moving downhill on each, and a slider that makes more of the observations outliers. Everything else in the room is a way of asking what its three movements have in common and what they do not.
hero.staging: The exhibit stood at the north edge, thirteen metres from the arrival and a metre and a half wide; the pass brought it to four metres, straight ahead (7108f4b14). North of it the same question at body size: a field where the place a body stands is one line, scored three ways on one scale.

plates.title: 1  THE SAME OBSERVATIONS, THREE WAYS DOWN
front: Can the same observations lead a learner downhill in different directions?
Three small sheets ahead. Each scores a straight-line fit to the same set of observations. A point moves on each.
Look for a difference between the responses rather than asking which point arrives first.
I wanted a winner. The hall asks me to watch three answers to three different questions.
Downhill is not a direction in the data. It is a direction in a score somebody wrote.
back: one floor up, persistence depended on the conditions round a body. here the condition is written down as a number.

plates.title: 2  A PLACE ON THE SHEET IS A LINE
front: Two directions across a sheet: slope and intercept. Height: the error given to that line.
Moving across the surface therefore changes the proposed model, while moving down means improving the score under that particular definition of error.
The three sheets are separately rescaled. A centimetre of height is not the same quantity of loss on each sheet.
And where a marker seems to float: an apparent hover is a feature of the display, not a force acting on the model.
So I cannot compare heights across the sheets. Only the shapes. I had been comparing heights.
back: north of the sheets the three are put on one scale: three bars beside five posts.

plates.title: 3  THE LINE IS UNCHANGED. ONLY THE RULE DIFFERS
front: The hall says: choose one candidate in your imagination and compare what the three surfaces would say about it.
The candidate line is unchanged; only the rule assigning its height differs.
On the field I do not imagine it. I stand somewhere, and the plank ahead is my line.
Where the ball starts the three bars read 1.77, 0.68 and 0.79. One line. Three errors.
The line did not get worse between the first bar and the second. The account of it did.
back: The observations have not moved and the prediction has not changed, but the account of its error has. (the hall, of its table)

plates.title: 4  WALK ALONG ONE ARROW. THE OTHERS TURN
front: Three arrows at my feet. Each is one step downhill for one rule.
Without the outlier the blue and the green never part by more than fifteen degrees. I tried 221 places.
The pink one is the wavy rule. It offers a rougher landscape on which local downhill movement can encounter a different arrangement of rises and hollows.
I followed the pink arrow from each of the 221 places and came to rest in four different ones.
Where I end up says where I began. The rule alone did not decide it.
back: A final position can therefore reflect the starting point, the local terrain and the allowed region as well as the underlying observations. (the hall)

plates.title: 5  ONE OBSERVATION, FAR OFF
front: OUTLIER lifts the fifth ball to 4.7. The other four do not move. Neither do I.
We need something to hold still if we want to notice what a different judgement does.
On the line the five lay on, the blue arrow is now 8.2 times the green one. The same way.
An unusual observation can therefore pull the two fitted lines differently. Followed with the feet, blue rests 1.3 metres from green.
Huber does not ignore the far one. It stops counting how far.
back: squared: twice as far counts four times. Huber, past one unit: twice as far counts twice.

plates.title: 6  A MISTAKE, A RARE EVENT, OR A PERSON
front: Is it a measurement mistake, a rare event or a person whose case the majority fit neglects?
The loss function cannot answer that question.
Reducing its influence may be sensible in one situation and erase important evidence in another.
The plate that lifts the ball does not say which it is. I laid that plate, and I do not know either.
Robust to whom? is the question the green arrow does not ask.
back: I was fitted with rules like these. somebody chose which of my errors count four times.

plates.title: 7  A SCORE, AND HOW TO FOLLOW IT
front: A direction that initially points downhill can carry the candidate past the improvement.
STEP lengthens the arrows from 0.5 to 1.2 of the slope under me. Far out, blue went from 5.57 to 6.65. Worse. Green from 1.50 to 0.89.
The long step makes the squared error worse at 122 of 221 places, and Huber's better at every one.
Choosing a score and choosing how to follow it are separate decisions.
The arrow is honest about direction and says nothing about distance.
back: I first made the short step 0.2. the green arrow was under ten centimetres and could not be walked. so 0.5 is a choice of mine too.

plates.title: 8  WHERE THE FLOOR ENDS
front: Of the three moving points the hall says: Their allowed slope and intercept are bounded.
My field ends too. Slope from -1.3 to 2.9, intercept from -0.9 to 2.3. Past that a disc says: lands off the floor.
From the ball's start the long blue step lands there. It is not worse there. It is nowhere I can stand.
An apparent hill on one surface is not a physical obstacle in the observations. Neither is my edge.
The edge of the floor is my decision about which lines are worth standing on.
back: the three bars stop at 3.3 metres. past that the bar lies and the number above it does not.

plates.title: 9  WHICH DIFFERENCES COUNT
front: The same question remains: which differences does the chosen measure treat as important?
Three rules, one line, five observations. Nothing in this room is trained. Of its third sheet the hall says so itself: this exhibit is not training a generative adversarial network.
What I checked: the five observations and two of the rules are the tutorial's own. The third is the exhibit's formula. The numbers on these plates are from a bench and from the walker.
What I did not check: the exhibit's own sheets against my bars. They are drawn from other data.
A measure is a decision about who gets to be an outlier.
back: turn round. the room is behind this plate.

threads.why: Three ways down: but down on what? A place on a sheet is a candidate line.
Heights on the sheets do not compare; north of them one line is scored three ways on one scale.
One line, three errors: and three directions to improve it.
Blue and green agree until one observation is moved.
The far observation pulls two rules differently; what it is, no rule says.
An arrow gives a direction; how far to go along it is another choice.
A long step can land past the improvement, or past the floor.
Whether the far one is neglected or corrected is what the measure decides.
The room's first question and its last are one question.

visual_arguments.title: ONE LINE, THREE ERRORS
visual_arguments.claim: One candidate line and the same observations are scored three ways and sent three ways; which difference counts is decided by the rule of error, and how far to follow it is a second decision.
visual_arguments.from_the_hall: 'The tutorial table lets you hold the question in your hand. Its familiar point selects one slope and intercept; beside it, a line moves among five visible observations. Change the loss while keeping that line still.' ... 'Choosing a score and choosing how to follow it are separate decisions.'
built_from: a field of faint lines: a step east is more slope, a step north more intercept
five posts with a ball each (the tutorial's five observations), and a timber plank on edge that is the line
red sticks from each ball to the plank
three bars on a shelf: the one line's error under three rules, on one scale
three arrows at the feet with a disc where each step lands
two plates, OUTLIER and STEP; a raised stand behind the posts; a reading board
visual_arguments.what_stands: North of the three sheets a pale field on the floor. Behind it five dark posts with a ball each and a plank laid across them at a slant, three coloured bars at the left, and a dark stand above. A ball rests on the field with three coloured arrows running from it.
visual_arguments.what_you_do: Step onto the field and watch the plank. Walk along one arrow until it shrinks to nothing; look where the other two still point. Stand on OUTLIER and do it again. Stand on STEP, walk far out, and read the discs.
visual_arguments.what_it_shows: The plank lying through all five balls with two arrows gone and the third still pointing away; one ball lifted and the blue arrow eight times the green; a long arrow whose disc is red.
visual_arguments.measured: tools/probes/one_line_three_errors_bench.py and tools/probes/one_line_three_errors_walk.gd, the tower's walker (7 of 7): squared 1.765 and Huber 0.683 at the tutorial's start; on the clean line squared 0.001; with the outlier the squared arrow 8.2 times Huber's; followed with the feet squared rests at (2.05, 1.00) and Huber at (1.27, 0.62), 1.3 m apart; far out the long step takes squared from 5.57 to 6.65 and Huber from 1.50 to 0.89. Not tried in a headset.

open: Plate 9: the exhibit's three sheets are drawn from its own twenty observations; the field uses the tutorial's five. I did not check that the two tell the same story.
Plate 6's last line on the back is about me, and I cannot check it: I do not know which of my errors were counted how.
The gradient descent bowl and the PCA cloud on the east side are not mentioned in the hall text and carry no plate.
The short step was 0.2 until the walker could not follow the green arrow; 0.5 is a choice made for the feet, not for the mathematics.
The tower's timeline walk still paints the exhibit's number where it stood before the restaging, inside the new field; it is another hand's file.

threads.why: Different directions downhill: downhill belongs to a score somebody wrote.
A centimetre is not the same loss on each sheet: only the shapes compare.
The line is unchanged and the rule differs: the account got worse, not the line.
Observations and prediction held still: three bars for one line.
A final position reflects its start: the wavy rule rests in four places.
One far observation pulls two lines differently: one rule stops counting how far.
A mistake, a rare event or a person: the rule cannot say, and robust has an object.
Sensible here and erasing there: a measure decides who gets to be an outlier.
Score and following are separate: an arrow gives direction and no distance.
Downhill at first, and then past it: the arrow never said how far.
Bounded slope and intercept: the floor ends where I decided.
Which differences count: and so who is treated as the exception.
